content: Three studies indicated that participants preferred having counseling available when using HIV self-testing (HIVST). However, 2% of participants expressed a preference for HIVST without counseling. Willingness to pay for an HIVST kit was documented in 11 studies, with variations depending on population, country income levels, specimen collection methods, and testing approaches. In high-income countries (HICs), participants were willing to pay between ≤US$20 and ≥US$50, while in middle-income countries (MICs), the range was generally between US$1 and US$20. Female sex workers (FSWs) were willing to pay slightly less than men who have sex with men (MSM) for HIVST kits. In supervised HIVST studies, participants were willing to pay between ≥US$1 and ≤US$20, whereas in unsupervised approaches, the willingness to pay ranged from ≥US$20 to US$50. Concerns about HIVST were reported in 11 studies, with the most common issues being user error, low accuracy, lack of counseling, and the cost of the test. These concerns were more frequently reported in studies using oral fluid-based rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). However, lack of counseling was not a concern in studies involving MSM and FSW participants. Six studies reported on linkage to care following HIVST, with most conducted in HICs. Two studies documented actual linkage to care, while others reported participants' intention to seek care. In one low-income country (LIC) study, 50% of MSM and 75% of FSWs stated they would seek post-test counseling and confirmatory testing after self-testing. Evidence on adverse events related to HIVST was limited, with one study reporting verbal confrontations or violence in specific circumstances, such as infidelity. No other serious adverse events were identified. The quality of studies varied, with many lacking sufficient information on qualitative methods and data collection tools. Most studies were observational and cross-sectional, with only one randomized controlled trial included. This heterogeneity in study design and incomplete reporting limited the generalizability of findings. Overall, MSM in HICs found oral fluid-based HIVST highly acceptable, whether supervised or unsupervised. However, concerns about counseling, user error, and accuracy remain. Data on social harm and adverse events were not well-documented, and further research is needed to address these gaps. The convenience and privacy of HIVST were seen as advantages, particularly for MSM, and may also benefit other key populations (KPs) such as FSWs, people who inject drugs (PWID), and transgender individuals. To increase uptake, HIVST may need to be subsidized or provided free of charge, especially in MICs and LICs.
